issuers.name: Another PingOne environment
issuers.what: A PingOne environment that issues access tokens. Trusting it lets one environment accept the other's tokens.
useWhen: Two PingOne environments, such as a development one and a production one, must honour each other's tokens.
A business unit with its own environment calls an API that lives in another.

gotchas.text: The issuer string carries the environment id as a path segment. Two environments differ only in that id.
PingOne ignores p1.userId on a token from a trusted issuer, so the person does not resolve to a user in the environment that accepts the token.

issuers.name: PingFederate
issuers.what: PingFederate as an OAuth and OIDC server. It issues ID tokens, access tokens and, since 13.1, ID-JAGs.
useWhen: You already run PingFederate as the authorization server and want its tokens, ID tokens or ID-JAGs trusted elsewhere.
A person signs in at PingFederate and an agent acts for them.

gotchas.text: A client-credentials token has exp but no iat and no nbf, so a Require Issued-at switch refuses it.
Our default access token manager issued opaque reference tokens. A surface that needs a JWT needs a JWT token manager with the audience and resource URI set.
PingFederate's ID-JAG header has no kid. A consumer that looks keys up by kid refuses it.

issuers.name: PingAM
issuers.what: PingAM, including PingOne Advanced Identity Cloud. Its issuer string includes the realm path.
useWhen: Your workforce or customer sign-in runs on PingAM or PingOne Advanced Identity Cloud and its tokens have to reach a PingOne API.
You protect an API with PingOne Authorize and the callers' tokens come from PingAM.

gotchas.text: The issuer is the realm URL, found through /oauth2/realms/root/.well-known/openid-configuration. A realm in the path is part of the string you must match.
The claim set shown here is our assumption, not a sample from Ping. Copy the claims from a real token before relying on it.

issuers.name: Okta
issuers.what: An Okta custom authorization server. The application id is cid and the scopes are scp.
useWhen: Your agents or apps sign in through Okta and the token has to be trusted by a Ping product.
You use Okta Cross App Access and need a Ping resource server to redeem its ID-JAG.

gotchas.text: An Okta token has no nbf, so a Require Not-before switch refuses it.
The calling application is cid, not client_id or azp. Map the right claim into act.

issuers.name: Auth0
issuers.what: An Auth0 tenant with its default access token profile.
useWhen: A customer-facing app signs in through Auth0 and calls an API that a Ping product guards.

gotchas.text: The issuer ends in a slash. Leave it off and the exact match fails.
aud is an array, and the token has no nbf and no jti.

issuers.name: Microsoft Entra ID (v1.0 and v2.0)
issuers.what: Microsoft Entra ID. The two token versions have different issuer strings and different claims.
useWhen: Your workforce signs in through Microsoft Entra ID and the token has to be trusted by a Ping product.
Both token versions are in use, so you need to trust both issuer strings.

gotchas.text: v1.0 ends in a slash and v2.0 ends in /v2.0. A surface that takes several Issuers needs both if you accept both.
The calling application is appid in v1.0 and azp in v2.0.

issuers.name: A generic RFC 9068 authorization server
issuers.what: Any authorization server that issues the standard JWT access token profile (RFC 9068).
useWhen: The other authorization server is not one we can name, but it issues standard JWT access tokens.
You want to check a product against the standard before testing it with a vendor.

gotchas.text: RFC 9068 requires iss, exp, aud, sub, client_id, iat and jti. It does not require nbf.
The access token header typ is at+jwt, which a surface that expects another typ would notice.

issuers.name: Kubernetes API server
issuers.what: A cluster's service-account issuer. A pod's projected token is its credential.
useWhen: An agent runs in a cluster and its projected service-account token should be its credential, with no stored secret.
A cluster-resident sensor reports to the Privilege gateway.

gotchas.text: The sub is system:serviceaccount:<namespace>:<name>. A live identity of ours had AllowAnySubject on: any pod in the cluster could present a token.
The audience on a projected token is chosen by whoever mounts it: bind the audience, never leave it to the default.

issuers.name: AWS EKS OIDC
issuers.what: The OIDC issuer of an EKS cluster. The issuer URL ends in a cluster id.
useWhen: The agent runs on EKS and the cluster's OIDC issuer is already set up for pod identity.
Two clusters must be trusted separately: each has its own issuer.

gotchas.text: Each cluster has its own issuer string: a token from cluster A must not satisfy an identity for cluster B. Our live identities pin the pod's service account.
The cluster id in the path is part of the exact match.

issuers.name: GitHub Actions
issuers.what: The OIDC issuer for CI jobs. Each job can request a short-lived token.
useWhen: A CI job has to call a gateway or a token endpoint with no stored secret, only the job's own token.
You want a release job trusted and a fork's pull request not trusted.

gotchas.text: The sub is composite (repository and ref). A surface that cannot pin claims cannot tell a release branch from a fork pull request: use RequiredClaims on repository, workflow, ref and environment.
The real issuer string is on the vendor's documentation. The host shown here is a stand-in on .example.

issuers.name: GitLab CI
issuers.what: The OIDC issuer for GitLab CI jobs.
useWhen: A GitLab pipeline has to call a gateway with no stored secret.
You want only one project and one branch trusted.

gotchas.text: The sub is composite (project path, ref type, ref). Pin project_path and ref with RequiredClaims where the surface allows it.
A self-hosted GitLab has its own issuer string. Use that host, not a shared one.

issuers.name: SPIFFE / SPIRE
issuers.what: A SPIRE server that issues JWT-SVIDs. The subject is the workload's SPIFFE ID.
useWhen: The estate mixes platforms and SPIFFE/SPIRE already gives every workload one identity.
You want the subject to be a SPIFFE ID, not a platform-specific name.

gotchas.text: The SPIFFE JWT-SVID rules require sub, aud and exp only. A surface that requires iat can refuse a token that has none.
The sub is a SPIFFE ID (spiffe://trust.example/path), not a URL you would put in an Issuer field.

issuers.name: Privilege Docker sensor (self-signed)
issuers.what: A shadow-AI sensor in Docker that signs its own token. The console pins the key's id, so the key file is the identity.
useWhen: A shadow-AI sensor runs in Docker and has to report to the Privilege gateway without a shared secret.

gotchas.text: Lose the key file and reports fail with Unauthenticated, because the console still pins the old key id. Paste the new key set; issuer, subject and audience do not change.
The audience is generated by the console (priv-nhi-<random>). Copy the one it issues.

issuers.name: Your own signer (private issuer)
issuers.what: An issuer you run whose keys are not reachable from the product, so its public keys are pinned instead of fetched.
useWhen: The issuer is yours and its keys cannot be fetched by the product, so you pin them.
You are testing a trust setting and want a token you control.

gotchas.text: With pinned keys, a rotation is a manual change in every product that trusts you. Plan the order: publish the new key first, then switch signing.
PingOne token exchange accepted a token from an issuer whose key we generated ourselves and pasted in as JWKS.
